metadata.title: A Spinning Top That Refuses to Fall
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: Gravity should topple a tilted top. Why does a spinning top circle instead of falling?
beats.new_visual_element: Portrait-only opening question card (title-styled, crimson underline).

beats.narration_text: Tilt a top away from the vertical and let go. If it is not spinning, gravity pulls it over and it falls. Spin it fast, though, and it does not fall. Its tilted axis slowly circles around the vertical instead. Why?
beats.new_visual_element: A wooden top (tan body, slate stripes, spindle) on a floor ellipse, tilted 25 degrees. First it is not spinning and topples onto the floor; it resets, spins (stripes and a curled spin arrow move), and its axis begins to circle the vertical. Crimson gravity arrow Mg at the center of mass.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: spinning, slowly precessing top on the floor, gravity arrow

beats.narration_text: Two vectors explain it. The spin gives the top an angular momentum, L, pointing along its axis. Gravity acts at the center of mass and produces a torque about the pivot, r cross M g. That torque does not point down. It is horizontal, perpendicular to both the axis and the force of gravity.
beats.new_visual_element: Precession pauses (spin continues). Teal L arrow along the spin axis beyond the spindle; dashed vertical reference line; gold torque arrow tau at the pivot, horizontal.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: spinning top, gravity Mg, L along axis, horizontal torque tau at pivot

beats.narration_text: Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum. In a short time, L changes by tau d t, in the direction of the torque. That change is perpendicular to L, so it does not tip L downward and does not change its length. It turns L sideways, at the same tilt.
beats.new_visual_element: Isolated diagram: L arrow from the pivot, a faded downward 'fall' arrow at its tip crossed out, the gold tau dt arrow perpendicular at the tip with a right-angle mark. L steps sideways three times, leaving faint copies along a horizontal arc.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: L, crossed-out fall direction, tau dt at tip, faint copies of earlier L along an arc

beats.narration_text: Apply that sideways nudge continuously, and the axis sweeps around the vertical, tracing out a cone. The torque turns along with it, always horizontal and always perpendicular to L. This steady circling of the spin axis is called precession.
beats.new_visual_element: Back to the full top: it precesses about the vertical; the tip of L traces a dashed horizontal circle and dashed cone edges; the torque arrow rotates with it.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: precessing top, L, tau, persistent dashed cone

beats.narration_text: Gravity never stops pulling. But on a spinning top its torque only keeps turning the axis sideways, so the top circles the vertical instead of falling over.
beats.new_visual_element: The top keeps precessing inside the dashed cone; label: torque perpendicular to L turns the axis, not the tilt.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: final: precessing top, dashed cone, L, tau, summary label
